p: On the thirty-first of October, fifteen seventeen, a professor of theology at the little university of Wittenberg in Saxony, an Augustinian friar named Martin Luther, sent to the Archbishop of Mainz a list of ninety-five propositions, or theses, for debate, concerning the sale of indulgences. Tradition says that he also nailed them to the door of the castle church, as was the custom for announcing an academic disputation; the Encyclopaedia notes that some scholars doubt the nailing, though nobody doubts the theses. He intended an argument among scholars. He began a revolution that divided Western Christendom permanently, set Europe at war with itself for more than a century, and made, by its consequences, a large part of the modern world.

To understand it, one must understand an indulgence. The Church of Rome taught that the sins of a Christian, even when forgiven, left a debt of temporal punishment to be paid, in this life or in purgatory after death; and that the Church, drawing on the infinite merits of Christ and the saints, could remit that punishment in return for prayers, pilgrimages or good works, including gifts of money to good causes. By the later Middle Ages, indulgences had become, in practice, a means of raising money, and the people were led to believe that they could buy release from purgatory for themselves and their dead relatives. In fifteen seventeen, the pope, Leo the Tenth, a son of the Medici family, was raising money to rebuild Saint Peter's in Rome, and a Dominican preacher named Johann Tetzel was selling indulgences in the lands near Wittenberg with a jingle that, in English, runs: as soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs.

There had long been complaints against the wealth, worldliness and corruption of the clergy: against bishops who held several sees and visited none, against popes who made war and enriched their families, against ignorant priests and idle monks. The English reformer John Wycliffe in the fourteenth century, and the Czech Jan Hus, burned for heresy in fourteen fifteen, had attacked the authority of the pope. Erasmus of Rotterdam, the greatest scholar of the age, had mocked the follies of the clergy with exquisite wit. But Luther's challenge went deeper than complaint.

Luther was a man of tormented conscience, who had become a friar after being terrified by a thunderstorm, and who had found no peace in all the disciplines of the monastery, being convinced that he could never do enough to satisfy a righteous God. His relief came, he said, from reading the letters of Saint Paul, in which he found that a man is justified, that is, made right with God, not by his works but by faith alone, as a free gift of grace. If that was so, then indulgences were not merely abused; they were pointless. So, in the end, were many things that the Church had taught for a thousand years: the merit of pilgrimages and relics, the special holiness of monks, the power of priests to forgive sins, and the authority of the pope himself, if it contradicted scripture. Luther came to hold that scripture alone was the final authority in religion, and that every Christian believer was, in a sense, a priest.

He was excommunicated by the pope in fifteen twenty-one, and summoned before the young emperor Charles the Fifth at the Diet, or imperial assembly, of Worms, to recant. He refused, saying, by the traditional account: here I stand, I can do no other, God help me. The emperor declared him an outlaw. He was saved by his own prince, the Elector Frederick of Saxony, who had him seized on the road by friendly kidnappers and hidden in the castle of the Wartburg, where in eleven weeks he translated the New Testament into German. His translation did for the German language what the Bible of King James would later do for ours.

His protest found support for many reasons, not all of them religious. German princes coveted the lands of the Church and resented the money flowing to Rome. The printing press, as I have said, carried his writings across Europe faster than the Church could answer them. Other reformers followed, more radical than he: Ulrich Zwingli in Zürich, and above all John Calvin in Geneva, a French lawyer of formidable logic, who organised a church governed by elders and a city disciplined by its ministers, and whose followers spread to France, the Netherlands, Scotland under John Knox, and among the Puritans of England. On the margins were the Anabaptists, who held that only adults should be baptised, and some of whom wished to abolish property and the state; they were persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike.

In England, the Reformation began, notoriously, with a king's desire for a divorce. Henry the Eighth, wanting a son and a new wife, and refused an annulment of his marriage by a pope who was in the power of his wife's nephew, the emperor Charles, broke with Rome in the fifteen-thirties, made himself Supreme Head of the Church of England, and dissolved the monasteries, whose lands he sold to his supporters. The doctrine of the English church swung to and fro under his children: Protestant under Edward the Sixth, Catholic under Mary, who burned some three hundred Protestants, and at last a middle way under Elizabeth, whose settlement is, broadly, the church in which I was baptised.

The Catholic Church responded with a reformation of its own: the Council of Trent, from fifteen forty-five, which defined its doctrine and reformed its abuses; new orders of great zeal, above all the Society of Jesus, the Jesuits, founded by a Spanish soldier, Ignatius of Loyola; and the Inquisition. Then came the wars. France was torn by civil war between Catholics and Protestants for thirty years, including the massacre of Saint Bartholomew's Day in fifteen seventy-two, when thousands of Protestants were murdered in Paris and the provinces. The Netherlands fought for eighty years to free themselves from Catholic Spain. And from sixteen eighteen to sixteen forty-eight, the Thirty Years' War devastated Germany so terribly that in some regions a third or more of the people died.

The Reformation ended with no victor. By the Peace of Westphalia in sixteen forty-eight, Europe accepted, wearily, that it would remain divided. And from that exhaustion, slowly, came the idea of toleration: that a state might contain subjects of different faiths, and that belief could not be compelled. Mr Locke wrote his Letter Concerning Toleration in sixteen eighty-nine. Some historians, following a German named Max Weber in the twentieth century, have argued further that the Protestant ethic of hard work and thrift helped to produce modern capitalism. Others doubt it. What is certain is that Luther, who wanted only to reform the Church, helped to unmake the medieval unity of Christendom, and that the individual conscience, standing alone before God and scripture, became a force in the world that no authority has since been able to contain.
